Paul measures uncertain imprisonment through the hearers' continuing need

Paul writes in chains and does not know the outcome (verses 13 and 20). Verse 21 says both outcomes are good to him. Verse 23 states his own wish: to depart and be with Christ. Verse 24 sets the readers’ need against that wish. To remain is “more needful” for them. Verse 25 says this convinces him that he will stay. His reason for staying is their progress and joy in the faith.
Christ's lowered position supplies the pattern for workers who serve others

Verse 3 forbids rivalry and conceit. Verse 4 states the same thing as a direction for the eyes. Each is to look to the things of others, not only his own. Verses 6–8 give the pattern: Christ did not grasp equality with God. He emptied himself and became obedient to death. The chapter then names two people who do this. Timothy cares for their state (verse 20), and Epaphroditus risked his life (verse 30).
Paul exchanges claims to rank for a pursuit he has not yet completed

Verses 5–6 give a proud record, and verse 7 calls it loss. Verses 10–11 say what he wants: to know Christ and reach the resurrection. Verse 12 stops any claim that he has arrived. He has not obtained it and is not yet perfect. Two verbs carry the verse. Paul presses on to take hold, because Christ first took hold of him. Verse 13 repeats the denial, and verse 14 keeps him running toward the prize.
Strength through Christ supports contentment within need and shared practical help

Verse 10 thanks the Philippians for their gift. Verse 11 at once says Paul does not speak from need. He has learned to be content in every state. Verse 12 names the states: hunger and plenty, abundance and want. “All things” in verse 13 means those conditions. Christ gives him strength to live through each one. Verse 14 still says they did well to share in his trouble.
